summaryEn: Taiwan's largest hazardous industrial-waste treatment company, whose moat is a near-unobtainable regulatory permit and scarce landfill capacity — an asset that depletes as it earns. Very high margins and 16 straight years of dividends, now transforming from burying waste toward a circular ecosystem of remediation, incineration and recycled materials.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press/company; waste-treatment framing — permit moat, ~50% gross margins and the 16-year dividend record credited, and the circular-economy transformation explained, while TWO data traps are corrected in full: the Oct-2025 1-for-10 split that makes raw databases show a fake '2025Q4 EPS -9.18' and a fake dividend cut, and the BOT construction-revenue recognition that inflated 2026 monthly revenue ~200%; landfill depletion, lumpy project revenue, negative BOT-driven cash flow and equity-diluted ROE stated plainly; distinguished from Australia's Cleanaway; sector/foundedYear/listedYear fixed)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Cleanaway Company (可寧衛, TWSE: 8422) is **Taiwan's largest treater of hazardous industrial waste** — and it has an economic structure unlike any other company in this collection. Its moat is neither technology nor brand: it is a **government permit that is almost impossible to obtain, attached to physical landfill capacity that depletes as the business earns**. When Taiwan was gripped by an illegal soil-dumping scandal, industry participants told the press they could find **only this one legally permitted operator** — which is the moat stated more plainly than any company could state it itself. Incorporated in **1999** as a joint venture involving Australia's Brambles (whose "Cleanaway" waste brand gives the company its name and its Chinese transliteration 可寧衛) and Taiwan's Kang Lien, renamed Cleanaway Company in 2009 and **listed in October 2011**, it is headquartered in Gangshan, Kaohsiung. *(It is a separate company from Australia's Cleanaway Waste Management, which shares the same Brambles-era brand ancestry.)*

The economics are what a scarce permit produces: a **gross margin around 48–53%**, an **operating margin of ~34%**, and **16 consecutive years of dividends** totalling more than NT$147 a share. Officially, FY2025 delivered **revenue of NT$4.78bn, net profit of NT$1.42bn, a 53% gross margin and record EPS**.

**Two accounting traps make the raw data actively misleading, and both need stating up front.** First, Cleanaway executed a **1-for-10 stock split in October 2025** (par value cut from NT$10 to NT$1; the ticker now carries an asterisk). Databases that derive quarterly EPS by subtraction therefore show a **catastrophic "2025Q4 loss of NT$9.18 a share" and an apparent dividend cut from ~NT$10 to NT$1.2 — both are pure artefacts** of mixing pre-split and post-split share counts. There was no loss (2025Q4 net income was **positive NT$277m**, and equity rose), and the dividend of NT$1.198 equals **~NT$12 pre-split — higher than recent years**. Second, monthly revenue leapt **~200% year-on-year in May 2026**, but this is **BOT construction-revenue recognition** on its incinerator project, not organic growth: it is low-margin and it **consumes cash** (2026Q1 operating cash flow was **−NT$1.22bn**). The honest read: **a high-margin, permit-protected, dividend-paying business with a genuinely rare moat — transforming from a depleting hole in the ground into a circular-economy operator, with a top line currently flattered by construction accounting and returns temporarily diluted by a large new joint venture.**

Cleanaway was **incorporated on 4 May 1999** to solve a problem Taiwan's industrial boom had created and no one wanted: **what to do with hazardous industrial waste**. It began as a joint venture combining **Australia's Brambles Industries — whose waste-management brand was "Cleanaway"** — with Taiwan's **Kang Lien (岡聯)**, and operated initially as **Cleanaway Kang Lien** before adopting the name **Cleanaway Company Limited in May 2009**. The Chinese name 可寧衛 is a phonetic rendering of "Cleanaway". It **listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange on 5 October 2011**.

The business it built is deceptively simple and extremely hard to copy. Hazardous waste from Taiwan's chemical, electronics and metal industries is **collected and transported**, then put through **intermediate treatment — solidification and stabilisation**, which locks contaminants into an inert matrix, and finally **buried in permitted landfill**. Every stage requires **environmental permits that Taiwan issues sparingly, and a physical site that no community wants nearby**. Over two decades Cleanaway assembled exactly that combination in **Kaohsiung**, the heart of Taiwan's heavy industry — and became the country's largest operator in the field.

The modern chapter is driven by an uncomfortable truth about its own model: **a landfill is a wasting asset**. Every tonne buried is capacity that can never be sold again. So Cleanaway has been converting itself from a **disposal** company into a **"zero-waste, resource-recovery"** one — moving upstream into **contaminated-soil remediation** (notably the large 205 Arsenal site in Kaohsiung), into **municipal waste-to-energy** through an incinerator **BOT joint venture with Taiwan Life**, and into **recycled aggregates and ready-mixed concrete**, so that material which once went into the ground comes back out as a product.

- **1999 (4 May)** — Incorporated as a JV involving Australia's Brambles ("Cleanaway") and Taiwan's Kang Lien (岡聯), based in **Gangshan, Kaohsiung**.
- **2000s** — Builds the full hazardous-waste chain: collection and transport → **solidification/stabilisation** → **permitted landfill**; becomes Taiwan's largest hazardous industrial-waste treater.
- **2009 (May)** — Renamed **Cleanaway Company Limited** (from Cleanaway Kang Lien).
- **2011 (5 Oct)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (8422)**.
- **2010s** — Establishes a long dividend record (NT$8–12 a share for over a decade) on ~50% gross margins; extends into recycled materials, power sales and concrete.
- **2025 (Oct/Nov)** — **1-for-10 stock split** (par value NT$10 → NT$1); new shares trade from 17 November.
- **2025 (FY)** — Record year: **revenue NT$4.78bn, net profit NT$1.42bn, 53% gross margin, EPS NT$1.29 post-split (≈NT$12.9 pre-split)**.
- **2026** — **205 Arsenal remediation** phases 2–3 land handed over from March; **southern-Kaohsiung incinerator BOT** (NT$15bn JV with Taiwan Life) takes over the old plant in January; **Dacheng recycled-aggregate plant** due to contribute from H2.

Cleanaway's accounts show a **high-margin, cash-generative licensed business** — but reading them requires knowing about two events that distort the raw numbers.

- **Trap 1: the 1-for-10 stock split (October 2025).** Par value was cut from **NT$10 to NT$1**, multiplying the share count tenfold; new shares began trading on 17 November 2025 (the ticker now displays with an asterisk). Databases that derive quarterly EPS by subtracting cumulative figures therefore report a **fictitious "2025Q4 EPS of −NT$9.18"** — the arithmetic of **NT$1.29 (full-year, post-split) minus NT$10.48 (nine-month cumulative, pre-split)**. In reality **2025Q4 net income was positive (NT$277m)** and **equity rose**. Likewise the dividend did **not** fall from ~NT$10 to NT$1.2: **NT$1.198 post-split equals ~NT$12 pre-split**, above recent years. **Sixteen consecutive years of dividends**, totalling over **NT$147 a share**, remain intact.
- **The real earnings record.** On today's post-split basis, annual EPS ran **NT$1.23 (FY2022) → 0.91 (FY2023) → 1.07 (FY2024) → 1.29 (FY2025, a record)** — multiply by ten for pre-split equivalents. FY2025 revenue was **NT$4.78bn** with a **53% gross margin** and **30% net margin**.
- **Trap 2: BOT construction revenue.** Monthly revenue spiked **~200% year-on-year in May 2026 (NT$1.27bn against a typical NT$0.3–0.6bn)** because of **construction-phase revenue recognition on the incinerator BOT** — low-margin, accounting-driven, and cash-consuming. It explains why **2026Q1 operating cash flow was −NT$1.22bn** despite healthy profits.
- **An enlarged capital base.** Total equity jumped from **NT$9.5bn to NT$12.5bn in a single quarter** as the **NT$15bn incinerator joint venture with Taiwan Life** came onto the balance sheet. That is why **ROE now reads ~10%**, below its historical level: profits have not yet caught up with the larger capital base.
- **Valuation.** At **NT$25.7**, the stock trades on **~23.8× earnings, ~2.7× book, with a ~4.7% yield** — priced as a quality, income-paying niche asset.

The financing reality: **a genuinely profitable, dividend-rich licensed business whose reported figures are currently distorted by a split and a construction-accounting cycle** — the underlying economics are far steadier than the raw data suggests.

**Stance: a permit-protected, high-margin niche monopoly-like asset with a 16-year dividend record, spending its scarce landfill inheritance to build a broader environmental franchise. The moat is real; the question is what replaces the hole in the ground.**

The bull case:

1. **A regulatory moat that competitors cannot buy.** Hazardous-waste permits and landfill sites are **near-impossible to obtain in Taiwan** — demonstrated vividly when, during the illegal soil-dumping turmoil, industry participants said they could find **only this one legally permitted operator**. That scarcity produces **~50% gross and ~34% operating margins**.
2. **A long, real dividend record.** **Sixteen consecutive years**, more than **NT$147 a share cumulative**, and a FY2025 payout equal to **~NT$12 pre-split** — higher than recent years — at a **~4.7% yield**.
3. **A credible transformation.** From burying waste toward a **circular ecosystem**: the **205 Arsenal soil remediation**, a **waste-to-energy incinerator BOT** (1,350 tonnes/day, 350m kWh a year when commercial), and **recycled aggregates feeding concrete** — each converting a disposal problem into a recurring or product revenue stream.

The counter-arguments are structural:

- **The core asset depletes.** Every tonne buried permanently consumes capacity. Without replacement permits, landfill revenue has a finite life — which is precisely why the transformation is not optional.
- **Lumpy project revenue.** The **205 Arsenal** project is a large, finite contract; management expects 2026's contribution to be similar to 2025's, but it ends eventually.
- **The BOT is a three-year cash drain before it pays.** The new plant reaches commercial operation in roughly three years while **construction consumes cash today** (2026Q1 operating cash flow −NT$1.22bn) and **inflates reported revenue** at low margin.
- **Diluted returns and reliance on regulation.** ROE has fallen to ~10% on the enlarged equity base, and the same regulatory regime that protects the moat could change the rules.

A **scarce-asset-in-transition** thesis: own it for the permit moat, high margins and income — while underwriting whether remediation, incineration and recycling can replace the landfill.

Cleanaway earns money by **taking custody of material nobody else is legally allowed to handle**, and increasingly by **turning that material back into products and power**:

- **Solidification and intermediate treatment — the core.** Hazardous industrial waste is chemically **solidified and stabilised** into an inert form suitable for disposal. This requires permits, process know-how and scale; it is the highest-margin step and the reason gross margins approach 50%.
- **Landfill — the scarce, depleting asset.** Treated material is buried in **permitted landfill**. This is the true bottleneck of the entire Taiwanese system: sites are almost impossible to permit, so whoever holds capacity holds pricing power. It is also a **wasting asset** — capacity sold is capacity gone.
- **Collection and transport.** The logistics front end that feeds the plants and locks in customer relationships.
- **Soil remediation — the project engine.** Cleaning contaminated and illegally dumped sites, most visibly the **205 Arsenal** project in Kaohsiung. High-value, but **contract-based and finite**.
- **Waste-to-energy — the recurring future.** The **southern-Kaohsiung incinerator BOT**, a **NT$15bn joint venture with Taiwan Life**: Cleanaway took over the existing plant in January 2026 and will run a new plant handling **1,350 tonnes a day and generating ~350m kWh a year**. During construction it generates **accounting revenue but consumes cash**; once operating it becomes a long-dated, contracted stream.
- **Recycled materials — closing the loop.** The **Dacheng recycled-aggregate plant** (contributing from H2 2026) turns residues into aggregate feeding **ready-mixed concrete** lines, alongside papermaking and power-sales segments; operations extend to China, Vietnam and Malaysia.

The economic logic: **a licence to handle what others cannot, monetised first by burying it and now by converting it.** The levers are **industrial waste volumes, permitted capacity, project wins, and the ramp of the incinerator and aggregate businesses**. The strength is a **regulatory moat with ~50% margins**; the structural challenge is that **the original asset literally runs out**, making the pivot to remediation, energy and recycled materials an existential requirement rather than an ambition.

Hazardous-waste treatment is an industry where **the competitive advantage is granted by government, not won in the market** — and Taiwan is an unusually extreme example.

- **Permits are the barrier, and they are scarce.** Taiwan is small, densely populated and environmentally sensitive; siting a hazardous-waste landfill or treatment facility requires approvals that are **politically difficult and rarely granted**. The result is a structurally short supply of legal capacity, and pricing power for incumbents. The clearest evidence came during the island's **illegal soil-dumping turmoil**, when industry participants publicly noted they could locate **only one legally permitted operator** to take the material.
- **Demand is created by regulation and industry.** Volumes come from Taiwan's **chemical, petrochemical, electronics and metal-processing** base, and rise with **enforcement intensity**. Crackdowns on illegal dumping directly convert grey-market volume into legal, paid volume — a regulatory tailwind that competitors cannot manufacture.
- **The industry is shifting from disposal to circularity.** Landfill space is finite everywhere, so environmental policy is pushing toward **incineration with energy recovery, soil remediation and material recycling**. That reshapes the industry from a real-estate-like model (own the hole) toward an **infrastructure and processing** model (own the plant, run it for decades) — which is exactly the transition Cleanaway is making via its BOT and aggregate projects.
- **Competition.** Rivals include other licensed treaters and incinerator operators (including BOT operators affiliated with engineering groups), but **no one can simply add capacity**; competition is for **contracts and permits**, not price wars.

Cleanaway's position is **as strong as regulation allows**: the largest licensed hazardous-waste treater in Taiwan, with capacity that is genuinely scarce. The industry truth is double-edged: **the same regulator that creates the moat sets the rules, prices and permits** — and the long-term direction of policy is away from burial and toward recovery, which rewards those who reinvest and punishes those who simply mine their landfill.

**Strengths**
- **Permit-based moat**: Taiwan's largest hazardous-waste treater; during the soil-dumping turmoil, reportedly the **only legally permitted operator** available.
- **Exceptional margins**: ~48–53% gross, ~34% operating, ~30% net (FY2025) — scarcity economics.
- **16 consecutive years of dividends** (>NT$147 a share cumulative); FY2025 payout ≈NT$12 pre-split, ~4.7% yield; record FY2025 profit.

**Weaknesses**
- **The core asset depletes** — landfill capacity sold is gone forever.
- **Lumpy project revenue** (the 205 Arsenal contract is finite) and a **cash-consuming BOT** build (2026Q1 operating cash flow −NT$1.22bn).
- **ROE diluted to ~10%** by the enlarged equity base after the NT$15bn JV; reported figures distorted by the split and construction accounting.

**Opportunities**
- **Waste-to-energy BOT** (1,350 t/day, ~350m kWh a year) becoming a decades-long recurring stream.
- **Soil remediation** demand as enforcement tightens; **recycled aggregates and concrete** closing the loop.
- Regional expansion (China, Vietnam, Malaysia); stricter enforcement converting illegal dumping into paid volume.

**Threats**
- **Regulatory change** — the rule-maker is also the moat-maker.
- **Permit renewal/expansion risk**; community opposition to siting.
- **Project execution** on the BOT and remediation contracts; industrial-production downturns reducing waste volumes.

- **Depleting landfill capacity (the structural risk).** Cleanaway's most profitable asset is finite by definition: capacity buried cannot be sold twice. If new permits or replacement capacity are not secured, the highest-margin revenue line has a limited life — which makes the transformation mandatory rather than optional.
- **Regulatory dependence, in both directions.** Permits create the moat, but the same authorities set rules, pricing constraints and renewal terms. Policy shifts (or a permitting decision) could materially change the economics.
- **Lumpy, finite project revenue.** The **205 Arsenal remediation** is a large contract with a defined life; management expects 2026 to resemble 2025, but such projects end, and replacing them is not guaranteed.
- **BOT execution and a three-year cash drain.** The incinerator reaches commercial operation only in roughly three years, while construction **consumes cash now** (2026Q1 operating cash flow −NT$1.22bn) and **inflates revenue at low margin** through construction accounting — flattering the top line while depressing quality.
- **Distorted reported figures.** The **1-for-10 split** makes naive quarterly data show a fictitious NT$9.18 per-share loss and an apparent dividend cut; investors relying on unadjusted screens will misread this company badly in either direction.
- **Diluted returns.** ROE has fallen to ~10% as equity expanded with the joint venture; it will only recover if the new assets earn their keep.
- **Cyclicality of waste volumes.** Hazardous-waste generation tracks industrial output; a manufacturing downturn reduces feedstock.

Cleanaway's outlook is a single strategic question: **can the circular businesses replace the hole in the ground before it runs out?** The axes to watch:

- **The incinerator BOT ramp.** The most important long-term driver — the **southern-Kaohsiung waste-to-energy plant** (NT$15bn JV with Taiwan Life) moving from **cash-consuming construction to commercial operation in roughly three years**, at **1,350 tonnes a day and ~350m kWh annually**. Success converts a depleting disposal model into **decades of contracted processing and power revenue**.
- **The 205 Arsenal project and remediation pipeline.** Phases 2–3 land was handed over from March 2026 and should contribute through year-end, with management guiding 2026 to resemble 2025 — but the strategic test is **what replaces it** when the contract ends.
- **Recycled materials.** The **Dacheng aggregate plant** contributing from H2 2026 and feeding a second concrete line — proof that residues can become products rather than landfill volume.
- **Reported-number quality.** Whether **construction-accounting revenue** is separated in investors' minds from organic operations, and whether **operating cash flow** returns to positive once the build phase passes.

Bottom line: Cleanaway owns one of the **rarest moats in this collection — a government permit and physical capacity that competitors cannot replicate**, producing **~50% gross margins and sixteen unbroken years of dividends**. But its core asset **depletes as it earns**, and its current figures are **doubly distorted** — by a **1-for-10 split** that makes raw data show a phantom loss and a phantom dividend cut, and by **BOT construction accounting** that inflates revenue while consuming cash. Judge it on **the incinerator BOT reaching commercial operation, the remediation pipeline beyond 205, and recycled materials scaling** — a scarce, high-margin, income-paying asset in the middle of converting itself from a place where waste ends into a business where waste is processed, recovered and sold again.
